full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman, J.:- This Rule arises out of a proceeding under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition & Tenancy Act and is directed against the appellate judgment and order reversing the judgment of the trial court. 

 4. During the pendency of this original application for pre-emption under section 96(1) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, one Oli Mia, the present opposite party No. 1 filed an application under section 96(4) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-emption and prayed therein for, his addition as opposite party No. 23. The case of the present opposite party No. 1 was that he was a co-sharer in the case land by purchase and no notice of the sale was served on him. The opposite party No. 1 for the first time came to know about the transfer on 20.10-73 from a notice Ext. B served on him regarding the pending pre-emption proceeding. The present opposite party No. 1 having a superior claim over the pre-emptor who is a contiguous landholder, filed that application under section 96(4) of the East Bengal state Acquisition and 'Tenancy Act and prayed for pre-emption with a prayer to make necessary deposit. 

 5. The learned Munsif allowed the application of the original pre-emtor and rejected the application of the couple, cant Oli Mia on 2 grounds namely, (1) the co-applicant failed to make the deposit at the time of filing of the application under section 96(4) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and (2) the application of the present opposite party No. 1 was barred by limitation as the same was not filed within 4 months from the date of transfer. 

 7. The present opposite party No. 1 Oli Mia also preferred an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 208 of 1976 against the order of the learned Munsif for rejecting his application under section 96(4) of the East Bengal State Acquisiton and Tenancy Act and the learned Additional District Judge by the impugned order allowed the application of the co-applicant Oli Mia and disallowed the original pre-emption case. 

 8. Mr. T.H. Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor has submitted two grounds for my consideration, firstly the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the application of the co-applicant under section 96(4) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is to be treated as a substantive application under section 96(1) of the East Bengal State Acquisition & Tenancy Act and in that view of the matter the co-applicant having not make the deposit as required under the law, the application of the co-applicant is liable to be dismissed. Lastly the learned Advocate for the petitioner has contended that the period of limitation as prescribed under section 96(4) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has not been properly construed by the lower appellate court and this has caused a failure of justice wherein an interference by this court in exercising its jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is called for. 

 9. In the instant case the pre-emptor filed the application for pre-emption under section 96(1) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, both as a co-sharer and as a contiguous landholder. Both the courts below on consideration of the evidence on record found that the pre-emptor is in fact a contiguous landholder and the co-applicant opposite party No. 1, Oli Mia is a co-sharer by purchase and in that view has a preferential claim for pre-emption over the contiguous land holder, the pre-emptor. Admittedly the co-applicant was not served with any notice under section 89 of the Act and the co-applicant was also not made a party in the proceeding. The co-applicant was brought on record after he was served with the notice Ext. B on 20.10.73. The case of the co-applicant was that on getting the notice of the proceeding he for the first time came to know about the proceeding and filed application under section 96(4) of the Act for joining as a co-sharer for pre-emption. 

 10. To appreciate the argument advanced from the Bar, it will be necessary here to refer to the relevant provisions of section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Sub-section (1) of Section 96 speaks that one or more co-sharer tenants of the holding within 4 months from the service of notice under section 89, or, if no notice has been given under that section within 4 months of the date of knowledge of the transfer may apply for pre-emption and a tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land so transferred may Me an application for pre-emption within 4 months from the date of knowledge of such transfer. Sub-section (3) (a) of section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act says that an application under section 96(1) shall be dismissed if no deposit is made in accordance with the provision of that sub-section. Sub-section (3) (b) of section 96 of the Act speaks of notice to the transferee and to other per-sons made parties under sub-section (2). Sub-section (4) of section 96 speaks that when an application has been made under sub-section (1) then the remaining co-sharer tenants and the contiguous landholder within the period of limitation as referred to in sub-section (1) or within 2 months of the date of service of notice of the application under Clause (b) of sub-section (3), whichever be earlier, may apply to join in the original application under this sub-section. Reading sub-section (1) of section 96 and sub-section (4) of section 96 of the Act it is clear that if the remaining co-sharer tenants or contiguous landholders do not join in the pre-emption proceeding then they will have no further right to purchase under the section. 

 13. Thus reading these various provisions of section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, it is clear that section 96 contemplates two distinct applications, one application under sub-section (1) of section 96 and, another application by the co-applicant or applicants under sub-section (4) of section 96 for joining with the original application under sub-section (1) within the period of limitation as provided is sub-section (4) of section 96 of the Act. Application under subsection (1) of section 96 speaks of a deposit under clause (a) of sub-section (3) of the Act which is mandatory and without the deposit the application shall be dismissed. But in the case of joining with the original application by the co-applicant or applicants under sub-section (4) of section 96 such deposit is not mandatory. Sub-section (4) of section 96 of the Act does not speak of any deposit along with the application of the co-applicant or applicants. The provision of clauses, (a)(b) of sub-section (6) makes it clear that on determination by the court the co-applicant under sub-section (4) shall deposit the amount. Thus it is abundantly clear from the plain language of the provision of the relevant sub-section as mentioned herein above that in an application under sub-section (4) of section 96 the period of such deposit is left with the discretion of the court and the order having been made by the court such deposit is to be made. Thus I have no hesitation in holding that a deposit as required under the law is mandatory under section (1) of section 96 whereas the deposit under sub-section (4) of section 96 of the Act is not mandatory and the same can be deposited subsequently as contemplated in clauses (a) (b) of sub-section (6) of section 96 of the Act. 

 19. For the reasons stated herein before and -in view of the fact that the lower appellate court has correctly decided the question of law and fact involved in this case, I find no reason for interference with the same.
